articles.title: Rochdale Opens New Children's Home 'Diamond' to Support Local Young People
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has inaugurated its fourth children's home, 'Diamond', as part of a £3.4 million investment to enhance local residential care for children with complex needs and disabilities.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has officially opened its fourth children's home, named 'Diamond', as part of a £3.4 million investment aimed at expanding residential care for children in the borough. This new facility is designed to support three children with complex needs and disabilities who come into care, providing them with a nurturing environment close to their community.

The home features a dedicated sensory room, which is intended to enhance the well-being of its young residents. With the addition of Diamond, the council now offers a total of 12 placements across four new homes, which also include 'Emerald', 'Sapphire', and 'Ruby'. These names were chosen following suggestions from children in care, reflecting their input in the development process.

Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children's services and education, expressed her delight at the opening, stating that the homely atmosphere of Diamond will significantly benefit the lives of children and young people in need of support. This initiative comes in response to a national challenge faced by local councils in securing suitable placements for children in care, allowing more young people to remain within their local area rather than being placed far from home.

The opening of Diamond is part of a broader strategy by Rochdale Borough Council to improve care services and ensure that children can grow up in a supportive and familiar environment. The council aims to continue enhancing its residential provision to meet the needs of its community.

A 39-year-old woman from Heywood has been arrested following a violent incident at Milnrow Cricket Club on April 2. Tara Hulme, known for her TikTok presence under the handle 'Heffer2020', was reportedly found drunkenly slumped in her seat at the club, prompting staff to ask her to leave.

According to Tameside Magistrates' Court, after being asked to exit the premises, Hulme became aggressive, slapping the bar manageress and spitting at two other staff members. The court heard that she also kicked a barmaid in the knee and punched another woman outside the pavilion, causing visible injury.

The incident escalated when a male club member intervened to stop the violence. Witnesses reported that families, including children, were present during the altercation, raising concerns about the safety of patrons at the family-friendly venue. One victim expressed feeling vulnerable and shocked by the incident, particularly given that it occurred in a workplace setting.

Hulme has a history of violence, with 19 previous offences, including an assault conviction from 2009. During the court proceedings, she claimed to have a 'vague' recollection of the events. The case highlights ongoing concerns regarding public safety in community spaces, particularly where families gather.

articles.title: Peacocks to Open New Store at Rochdale Riverside as Footfall Increases by 15.3%
articles.excerpt: British clothing retailer Peacocks has signed a long-term lease for a unit at Rochdale Riverside, contributing to a 15.3% rise in footfall at the shopping centre.
articles.content_html:
British clothing retailer Peacocks has secured a long-term lease for a 10,181 sq ft unit at Rochdale Riverside, which is now 92% occupied. The store is set to open at the beginning of October 2026, further enhancing the shopping and leisure offerings at the centre.

The announcement follows a significant 15.3% increase in footfall at Rochdale Riverside, with nearly 200,000 visitors recorded in July alone. This upward trend in visitor numbers has been consistent throughout 2026, indicating a growing interest in the retail destination since its opening in Spring 2020.

Rochdale Riverside, which spans 200,000 sq ft, features a mix of shopping, dining, and leisure options, anchored by a 50,000 sq ft Marks & Spencer store and a six-screen Real Cinema. Other national retailers at the centre include Next, H&M, Boots, and JD Sports. Ollie Holland, asset manager for Rochdale Riverside at RivingtonHark, expressed confidence in the centre's appeal, stating that the addition of Peacocks reflects strong demand for well-located retail space.

Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for regeneration and housing at Rochdale Borough Council, welcomed the new store, noting that it would be a popular addition to the shopping centre. Peacocks, established in 1884 and now operating 345 stores across the UK, is known for its budget-friendly clothing options, which will complement the existing retail mix at Rochdale Riverside.

This disruption may affect local commuters and those travelling to and from Rochdale, so passengers should plan their journeys accordingly.

articles.title: Digital Autopsy Service Launched to Reduce Invasive Post-Mortems in Heywood and Surrounding Areas
articles.excerpt: The Coroner’s Office for Greater Manchester has introduced a digital autopsy service that could reduce the need for invasive post-mortems by up to 80%, providing families with a less distressing option during their time of grief.
articles.content_html:
The Coroner’s Office for Greater Manchester has launched a pioneering digital autopsy service that aims to reduce the need for invasive post-mortems by up to 80% across Rochdale, Bury, and Oldham. This innovative service, developed in partnership with the NHS, specialist post-mortem imaging provider Anubix, and medical imaging provider TIC Health, seeks to offer families a less distressing alternative during their time of grief.

The service will employ computed tomography (CT) scanning to help determine the cause of death without the need for traditional invasive procedures. This approach is expected to alleviate additional anxiety for families, as invasive post-mortems can often cause further distress during an already difficult time. A number of scans will be conducted each week, with the long-term goal of expediting the process for families following the loss of a loved one.

Councillor Neil Emmott, leader of Rochdale Borough Council, expressed support for the initiative, stating that it is a sensitive issue that has been handled with care. He noted that many residents in Heywood, Middleton, Pennines, and Rochdale have raised concerns about the distress caused by invasive post-mortems, making this new service a timely and welcome development.

Joanne Kearsley, senior coroner for Manchester North, highlighted the importance of this advancement in the coroner’s service, which aims to provide the best possible support for families. The introduction of digital autopsies represents a significant step forward in modernising the coroner’s service and improving the experience for bereaved families in Heywood and the surrounding areas.

articles.title: Who — or what — is the Healey Dwarf? Tracing the legend from Roby to the Heritage Centre
articles.excerpt: A guide to the small ginger‑bearded figure said to haunt Healey Dell, showing what the old printed collectors recorded, what later Victorian writers added, and what is verifiable today.
articles.summary: A guide to the small ginger‑bearded figure said to haunt Healey Dell, showing what the old printed collectors recorded, what later Victorian writers added, and what is verifiable today.
articles.body:
Healey Dell is home to one of Rochdale borough’s most persistent pieces of local folklore: a small, bearded figure associated with the fairies and a feature known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel. The figure is usually called the Healey Dwarf in modern storytelling — a sentinel‑like stone or a tiny person who met the Fairy Queen — but the story we hear walking the Spodden today is the result of at least two centuries of retelling rather than a single documentary record.

The oldest readily available printed versions come from early nineteenth‑century folklore collecting. John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire (first published 1829–31) includes a long set of tales about Healey, “The Fairies’ Chapel” and the nearby cleft called the Thrutch; Roby’s chapters record the local romance‑style narratives then circulating and helped fix many of the plot elements later writers used. Roby’s work is a literary‑folklore source: it records what people were telling but is not a neutral archival record of events. For dating, Roby’s collections are the earliest printed witnesses I was able to locate. ([arc-codex.com](https://www.arc-codex.com/library/25256))

Later Victorian writers took up Roby’s materials and embellished them. A specifically titled book, Healey Dell, or The History [in Verse] of Fairies: Meetings of the Fairy Queen and Healey Dwarf in the Fairy Chapel, appeared in 1882 (R. Standring). Standring’s work is a clearly literary and romantic reworking: it gives a full narrative about a character called Healey (described in jaunty costume with a ginger beard) being offered a place among the fairies and taking the form of a stone guardian in the river. That 1882 text is an important source for how the dwarf appears in later local guidebooks and family storytelling. ([books.google.com](https://books.google.com/books/about/Healey_Dell_Or_The_History_in_Verse_of_F.html?id=IYMNAAAAYAAJ))

How the story sits with the place you can visit today is straightforward to separate. Healey Dell is a documented nature reserve and visitor attraction with industrial archaeology (old mills and a prominent Victorian viaduct) and a heritage centre that interprets the site for visitors. The borough’s directory entry and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre both explain the real, physical origin of the Fairies’ Chapel name: the River Spodden has carved a niche in the rock (a pulpit‑like alcove and seats) that easily invited imaginative readings as a tiny “chapel” of the fairies, and Victorian tourists specialised in that kind of romantic topography. Those facts about the reserve and its facilities are supported by Rochdale Borough Council’s site listing and the heritage centre’s material. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

Modern retellings at the heritage centre and in local guides often weave Roby and Standring together, and sometimes add Victorian‑era motifs (a prophetic Fairy Queen; witches turned to stone; prophetic local fortunes). The centre openly treats these stories as legend and performs them for visitors — for example, the site’s guide materials and a short printed “Fairies’ Chapel” guide present the Healey Dwarf story as part of the Dell’s folklore rather than as a historical event. Erosive geology and historic floods are cited to explain why the rock shapes and river features described by nineteenth‑century writers may not look identical now. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

What we can say with confidence, and what we should treat as folklore: facts — the place, the rock niche, the industrial remains, the viaduct and the existence today of a heritage centre and nature reserve — are verifiable; the Healey Dwarf as a supernatural person or as a stone sentinel with fairy agency is a narrative motif preserved in nineteenth‑century collections and in later local retellings. Roby (1829–31) and Standring (1882) are the best early printed witnesses of the tale; later accounts draw on them and on the Dell’s Victorian reputation as a beauty spot. If a claim cannot be found in archival records or contemporary documentary sources (for example, a dated eyewitness affidavit or an official inspection reporting “a dwarf”), it should be treated plainly as folklore and local tradition rather than as documented fact. ([arc-codex.com](https://www.arc-codex.com/library/25256))

If you go looking for the Healey Dwarf today, bring an appetite for both geology and story. Stand by the Thrutch and you’ll see the water‑carved niche that inspired the “Fairies’ Chapel” name; follow the heritage centre’s displays for the Victorian and folkloric layers of the tale; and read Roby if you want the earliest printed atmosphere of the story that fixed many of the characters and episodes. Where Roby and Standring record what people told in the nineteenth century, the modern council and heritage‑centre material remind visitors we are dealing with cultural memory and storytelling as much as with stones and riverbeds. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

articles.title: Middleton Residents Campaign to Preserve Kickpitch Amid Plans for Car Park
articles.excerpt: Residents of the Langley Estate in Middleton are actively campaigning to retain their community kickpitch, which is set to be replaced by a car park for the Burnside Centre.
articles.content_html:
Residents in the Langley Estate of Middleton are campaigning to keep their community kickpitch, which is slated for removal to make way for a car park. The pitch, located on Burnside Crescent next to the Burnside Centre, serves as a vital hub for local sports and community activities.

The decision to decommission the pitch comes as part of plans to create a car park for the Burnside Centre. Families have expressed concerns, stating that the pitch is an essential space for children and young people to engage in football and other sports. The pitch is one of three on the estate, and campaigners are advocating for a new facility to be built on adjacent land rather than losing the existing one.

Residents have been informed that replacement facilities will be available at Rochdale AFC and the planned Football and Community Wellbeing Hub at Bowlee Playing Fields. However, many feel that these alternatives do not adequately replace the local access and community spirit fostered by the existing kickpitch.

The Burnside Centre has acknowledged the community's disappointment, citing concerns over antisocial behaviour and the pitch's deteriorating condition as reasons for the decision. The centre noted that the pitch, established in the late 1990s, had reached the end of its expected lifespan and required significant investment to remain operational. Local resident Kelly Burton, a mother of four, emphasised the importance of the pitch as a safe space for children to meet and play together.

articles.title: Ex-Prisoner Jamie Dale Advocates for Support in Early Release Scheme
articles.excerpt: Jamie Dale, a former prisoner from Rochdale, emphasises the need for support from ex-offenders in government plans for early inmate release to prevent reoffending and homelessness.
articles.content_html:
Jamie Dale, a former prisoner from Rochdale, has voiced concerns regarding the government's plans to release inmates early as a measure to alleviate prison overcrowding. Dale, who spent over 11 years in prison for his involvement in organised crime, now runs the Old Lags Network, a support initiative aimed at helping ex-offenders reintegrate into society.

Dale argues that the success of such early release schemes hinges on the involvement of individuals who have experienced the prison system firsthand. He believes that without adequate support, many released prisoners may struggle to adjust, leading to a high rate of reoffending. "Most of the people who return quite quickly have not got great family networks," he stated.

The Old Lags Network, established in September 2025, focuses on bridging the gap between prison and community, aiming to reduce the number of individuals who fall through the cracks after their release. Dale emphasised that many ex-offenders end up homeless, which exacerbates the cycle of reoffending. He believes that including ex-prisoners in the development of support solutions could significantly decrease the number of individuals recalled to prison.

As the government continues to explore early release options, Dale's insights highlight the critical need for comprehensive support systems that address the challenges faced by former inmates. His advocacy underscores the importance of community involvement in creating effective rehabilitation pathways.

articles.title: Ian Watson Praises Rochdale AFC Performance in Trophy Tie Against Liverpool Under-21s
articles.excerpt: Rochdale AFC faced Liverpool Under-21s in an exciting Jersey Mike's Trophy match, ending in a 3-3 draw before Liverpool triumphed 7-6 on penalties.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC played to a thrilling 3-3 draw against Liverpool Under-21s in the Jersey Mike's Trophy on Tuesday night, with the match ultimately decided by a penalty shootout that saw Liverpool prevail 7-6.

The game took place at Rochdale's home ground, where the hosts took advantage of Liverpool's Mor Talla Ndiaye being sent off midway through the first half. Devante Rodney opened the scoring for Rochdale with a well-placed shot from distance in the 37th minute, but Liverpool equalised just before half-time through a remarkable solo effort by Will Wright in the 42nd minute.

Rochdale regained the lead with two goals from Ian Henderson, who scored in the 74th and 90th minutes, putting them ahead 3-1 as the match approached stoppage time. However, Liverpool's substitutes Ben Trueman and Josh Sonni-Lambie scored in quick succession in the 90+1 and 90+3 minutes to level the match at 3-3, forcing the game into penalties.

In the shootout, both teams displayed strong performances, but Liverpool secured the bonus point with a 7-6 victory. This match marks an exciting start for both teams in the Jersey Mike's Trophy, showcasing the competitive spirit of youth football.
